sections.h2: Can Marion County owners pay their property tax in quarterly installments?
sections.html:
Yes, if they enroll on time. The Marion County Tax Collector's installment page wants Form DR534 on file ahead of May 1 in the year you join, and the prior year's bill has to have topped $100.

Once enrolled, an owner does not reapply each year, with one catch: if the first installment is missed, the account drops out and the owner has to reapply by April 30 of a later year. Four payments follow a fixed pattern, and the first two are based on the previous year's gross tax.

Marion County installment schedule as printed by the Tax Collector
PaymentDueAmountDiscount
FirstJune 30One quarter of last year's gross tax6%
SecondSeptember 30One quarter of last year's gross tax4.5%
ThirdDecember 31One quarter of this year's adjusted tax3%
FourthMarch 31One quarter of this year's adjusted taxNone

Source: Marion County Tax Collector, installment plan.

A late first payment can still be made by July 31, though without the discount. After July 31 the account reverts to ordinary annual billing.

Compare that with the ordinary route. A lump sum paid in November earns 4%, and the cut falls a point each month to 1% in February. Quarterly payers collect larger percentages on early installments but pay across a whole year, so the plan suits owners who prefer smooth cash flow over one big bill. A seller weighing the plan against an upcoming listing should remember that the discounted amounts are tied to last year's bill, which can differ from what the new year's roll produces.

sections.h2: What happens to a Marion installment plan when the house sells?
sections.html:
The plan belongs to the tax year, not to the seller. According to the collector, a property that changes hands after one or more quarterly payments must stay on the plan for that year under the new owner.

So a half-paid plan travels with the house. A buyer inherits the remaining quarters, and your title company needs to see which ones were already paid. Request a payment history from the collector and pass copies to both sides.

  • Put the plan details in the disclosure packet so no one finds them at the closing table.
  • Check that the settlement statement credits installments you already covered.
  • A buyer who prefers one annual bill should ask the collector whether the account can revert.

sections.h2: Where do Marion County sellers go in person for tax questions?
sections.html:
The Tax Collector keeps offices around the county, each open Monday to Friday from eight to four. Tax deed and certificate questions go only to the main branch, which matters if your parcel has an old balance.

  • Main office, McPherson Complex, 503 SE 25th Avenue, Ocala.
  • Dunnellon, inside the Rainbow Springs Government Complex.
  • Belleview, in the Belleview Regional Shopping Center on U.S. 441.
  • Forest, at Forest Center on State Road 40 in Silver Springs.
  • State Road 200, at Jasmine Square in Ocala.
  • North, at Ocala Springs Shopping Center on U.S. 441.
  • Summerfield, at Spruce Creek Terrace Shops.
  • Ocala Annex, which serves driver license customers only.

The office suggests midweek visits, ideally between 9:30 and 10:30 in the morning, and warns that Mondays, Fridays and month-end days run busiest. Lobby cameras on its site show the line before you leave. The shared number is (352) 368-8200.

sections.h2: Which Marion offices handle value, billing and records?
sections.html:
Three offices touch a Marion sale, and each owns a different question. All sit in Ocala, though each keeps its own website and search tools.

The Property Appraiser at 501 SE 25th Avenue determines value and processes exemptions, taking walk-ins or booked appointments. The Tax Collector issues and collects the bill. The Clerk of Court and Comptroller records deeds, hosts the Value Adjustment Board filings and conducts deed sales.

The statewide calendar sits on top of all three: January 1 fixes ownership and condition, March 1 closes exemption filings, April 1 is the tangible personal property deadline, and the proposed-tax notice lands in August. The collector's payment page gives November 1 as the due date.

sections.h2: Do Marion vacation rentals owe a separate local tax?
sections.html:
Yes. Rentals of six months or less carry a 4% Tourist Development Tax, collected from the guest and sent to the Tax Collector. The collector's page adds that Marion County has no contract with platforms such as Airbnb or VRBO, so the owner has to register, collect and remit directly.

The same page puts state sales tax at 7.5% in Marion County, made up of 6% plus a 1.5% infrastructure surtax. The tourist tax applies to rent and to fees tied to the stay, such as cleaning and pet fees.

  • The return is due on the first of the following month and is late after the 20th.
  • Operators file each month, collections or not.
  • Lateness costs 10% of the tax for each month, with a $50 floor and a ceiling of half the tax due.
  • An owner who sells or closes the business should notify the office in writing.

Past guest stays leave a paper trail. Pull your registration number, monthly returns and proof of payment together, because a careful buyer will want to see that the account is current.

sections.h2: What can the Marion appraiser's website do for a seller?
sections.html:
The site bundles a tax estimator, a request form for a mortgage estimate letter, a change-of-address form and a homestead e-file page. It adds a damage report page and a confidential channel for tips about suspected homestead fraud.

Run the estimator at a realistic sale price. A sale resets assessed value, so the buyer's first bill can differ sharply from yours, and lenders ask about that gap. Homestead trims up to $50,000 from the taxable base, with only the first $25,000 applying to school taxes, and the state cap protecting your own assessment ends at transfer.

After you move, file the address change. Notices follow the address on record, and a bill that never arrives still has to be paid.

sections.h2: What happens when Marion County taxes go unpaid?
sections.html:
April 1 marks the shift from routine billing to collection. Delinquent parcels are advertised, and certificates are sold by June 1. A certificate buyer covers the bill and collects interest, yet cannot demand money from the owner for two years.

The collector's menu offers an online tax deed application, online purchase of county-held certificates and a delinquent tax page. Homestead parcels start higher at a deed sale. Paying off a certificate sooner costs less, because interest keeps building.

sections.h2: Can a Marion County house with taxes owed still be sold?
sections.html:
Yes. Back taxes are common in estate sales and in houses left empty, and buyers expect them. Get the exact balance from the collector, and the closing agent deducts it from what the buyer brings.

The state charges seventy cents on each hundred dollars of price in deed stamps, paid at the clerk's recording desk. With an inherited house or several unpaid years, secure a written payoff before you accept anything. The Clerk's Property Alert Service sends a message whenever a document is recorded under your parcel or name, which helps spot deed fraud.

faqs.q: Who sends the Marion County tax bill?
faqs.a: The Marion County Tax Collector. The Property Appraiser sets the value but never mails a bill, and the Clerk records deeds and handles deed sales.

faqs.q: What is the first Marion installment due date?
faqs.a: June 30, with a 6% discount on one quarter of last year's gross tax. A late first payment is allowed through July 31 without the discount.

faqs.q: Does the buyer keep my Marion installment plan?
faqs.a: Yes for that tax year. The collector states that a new owner must continue on the plan if the property sells after payments have started.

faqs.q: Do Marion vacation rentals pay a tax beyond sales tax?
faqs.a: Yes, a 4% Tourist Development Tax on rentals of six months or less, paid to the Tax Collector by the owner because no platform contract exists.

faqs.q: Where can I ask about a tax certificate in Marion County?
faqs.a: At the main Tax Collector office, 503 SE 25th Avenue, Ocala. The branch page says only the main branch handles tax deed and certificate information.
